[u1]
## Operating the pool

### Sizing the pool

Each Ledger instance runs a pool of at most 20 connections. The database accepts 400 connections in total, and 40 of those are reserved for migrations and administrators. That leaves room for 18 instances at full size, so the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances. Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection; once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower. A pool sized for peak traffic also holds idle connections at night, which costs memory on the database but nothing else.

### Timeouts

A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with `POOL_EXHAUSTED`. The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller still has time to return a clear error. Each query also has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with `SET statement_timeout = '3s'` when the connection is opened. The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit. A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.

### Health checks and failover

Before lending a connection that has been idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs `SELECT 1` to check that it still works. A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one. During a database failover, every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary. Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance, so that 18 instances reconnecting together don't overload the new primary. Until the pool is refilled, requests may see `POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors for up to about 4 seconds.

### Connection leaks

A connection that stays borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, together with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it. The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it. Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection. Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.

### Watching the pool

The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow. An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row. A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not with the pool size. The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a failover has finished.

Design the structure of a visual knowledge workspace for the content below. The content is split into numbered parts ([u1], [u2], …) at its headings.

Group the parts into sections by MEANING, not by the source's headings — headings are hints only:
- Merge parts that describe the same concept or the same set of entities (e.g. plans described in several places become ONE comparison section).
- Every part belongs to exactly one section, and every part is used. Never invent content.
- Give each section a short label (at most 5 words) in the content's own words; a section that is one part keeps that part's own heading.

Classify each section by asking, in this order, and taking the first that fits:
- "comparison": several entities (options, plans, tiers, products, alternatives) described by the same attributes, even when those facts are scattered across the text — including a change described case by case: how several cases, inputs or checks behaved before and how they behave now (old vs new, v2 vs v3)
- "hierarchy": a hierarchy, branching, categorisation or parent/child structure (A contains or branches into B), including an ASCII/box-drawing tree
- "flow": a sequence: steps, stages or a chain of cause and effect, where the order is the point
- "cards": 2–6 parallel, independent concepts of similar weight, each short (personas, categories, principles, options without shared attributes)
- "decision": a recommendation, decision, conclusion or chosen direction — including a set of decisions or proposals (D1, D2, …; question → proposal), even when they are numbered
- "metrics": numbers, measurements, metrics, costs or things to track
- "annotated": running prose where specific phrases or claims need their own explanation, caveat or source attached, without breaking the prose into cards
- "supporting": reasoning, evidence, examples, caveats or background that supports another section rather than being a main idea
- "notes": anything else

A "flow" is only for steps where each one leads to the next. Numbered or listed items that stand on their own (decisions D1, D2 …, options, requirements, findings) are not a flow, even in a numbered list.

Mark a section "primary" when it carries a main idea (the structure, the comparison, the decision) and "supporting" when it is reasoning, evidence, examples or detail. Order sections so the main ideas come first: what this is, the main structure or comparison, the decision; supporting sections after them.

Add links between sections only where the content states or clearly implies a relationship, using these types: "relates_to", "flows_to", "caused_by", "depends_on", "supports", "blocks", "implements", "derived_from", "references", "explained_by", "supersedes", "deviates_from", "option_of", "calls", "reads", "writes", "publishes", "subscribes", "contains".
Add a one-line summary of the whole content (at most 15 words, e.g. "Free product + limited AI → Pro → optional BYOK").

[u1] (Running a shared connection pool › Why pool connections)
## Why pool connections

Opening a new database connection costs the Ledger service about 30 ms, because each one needs a TLS handshake and an authentication round trip. A pool keeps a set of connections open and lends them to requests, so most requests skip that cost entirely. The pool also caps how many connections the service can hold, which protects the database from a traffic spike.

## Takeaway

A pool makes connections cheap and bounded, but its size, its timeouts and its failover behaviour have to be set together with the database's own limits.

## Operating the pool

### Sizing the pool

[P1]
P1.1 Each Ledger instance runs a pool of at most 20 connections.
P1.2 The database accepts 400 connections in total, and 40 of those are reserved for migrations and administrators.
P1.3 That leaves room for 18 instances at full size, so the autoscaler is capped at 18 instances.
P1.4 Raising the pool size only helps while requests are waiting for a connection; once the database CPU is saturated, more connections make every query slower.
P1.5 A pool sized for peak traffic also holds idle connections at night, which costs memory on the database but nothing else.

### Timeouts

[P2]
P2.1 A request waits at most 2 seconds to borrow a connection before it fails with `POOL_EXHAUSTED`.
P2.2 The wait limit is deliberately shorter than the 5-second request deadline, so the caller still has time to return a clear error.
P2.3 Each query also has a statement timeout of 3 seconds, set with `SET statement_timeout = '3s'` when the connection is opened.
P2.4 The statement timeout does not apply to migrations, which run on their own reserved connections without a limit.
P2.5 A long transaction holds its connection for its whole duration, so the team keeps transactions under 500 ms.

### Health checks and failover

[P3]
P3.1 Before lending a connection that has been idle for more than 60 seconds, the pool runs `SELECT 1` to check that it still works.
P3.2 A connection that fails the check is closed and replaced, and the request gets a fresh one.
P3.3 During a database failover, every open connection breaks at once, so the pool is drained and refilled from the new primary.
P3.4 Refilling is limited to 5 new connections per second per instance, so that 18 instances reconnecting together don't overload the new primary.
P3.5 Until the pool is refilled, requests may see `POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors for up to about 4 seconds.

### Connection leaks

[P4]
P4.1 A connection that stays borrowed for more than 10 seconds is logged as a possible leak, together with the stack trace of the code that borrowed it.
P4.2 The pool does not take a leaked connection back by force, because the code holding it may still be using it.
P4.3 Most leaks the team has found came from error paths that returned early without releasing the connection.
P4.4 Leak warnings are reviewed every week, and a leak that comes back gets a ticket for the team that owns the code.

### Watching the pool

[P5]
P5.1 The pool exports three gauges: connections in use, idle connections, and requests waiting to borrow.
P5.2 An alert pages the on-call engineer when requests have been waiting for more than 30 seconds in a row.
P5.3 A sustained queue usually means slow queries rather than a pool that is too small, so the runbook starts with the slowest statements, not with the pool size.
P5.4 The idle gauge drops to zero during a failover and recovers as the pool refills, which makes it a quick way to confirm that a failover has finished.
